body: Garden Monitor --- 🎯 Today's Focus - First comprehensive post-transplant health check on all outdoor plants. - Document lime tree pest pressure (slug slime + citrus leaf miner damage). - Confirm carrot crop status (presumed lost). - Build per-plant log files for ongoing tracking. ✅ Done - Full visual health audit of every outdoor zone: 3 tomatoes, 2 bell peppers, 4 onions, potato tower, watermelon, 4 corn stalks, lime tree, lavender planter, citronella, and the carrot bucket. - Confirmed: 50% shade cloth has been deployed over the raised bed for ~2 weeks — protecting tomatoes/peppers/onions ahead of the impending peak heat window. - Lime tree pest diagnosis: Two concurrent issues identified — surface slime from slugs/snails climbing up at night, and citrus leaf miner larvae tunneling inside new flush growth (visible as silvery squiggles inside cupped/curled leaves). Endemic in Houston citrus. - Carrot crop declared dead. Four planted, zero germinated. Postmortem: wrong season for Houston (cool-season crop sown in April → soil too hot for germination), heavy straw cover likely smothered fine seeds, container surface dry-out during the 14–21 day germination window. - Per-plant care logs created for vault: Tomato, Bell Pepper, Onion, Potato Tower, Watermelon, Corn, Citronella, Lavender, Carrot (memorial), and Lime Tree. Each includes latest observation, health rating, immediate + ongoing actions, and a history table. 📝 Notes Health snapshot summary: | Plant | Health | Trend | |-------|--------|-------| | Potato Tower | 🟢 Excellent | ⬆️ | | Corn (4 stalks) | 🟢 Excellent | ⬆️ | | Bell Pepper #1 | 🟢 Excellent | ⬆️ | | Lime Tree | 🟢 Excellent (under pest pressure) | ⬆️ | | Tomatoes (3) | 🟡 Fair — recovering | ➡️ | | Bell Pepper #2 | 🟡 Fair — lagging | ➡️ | | Watermelon | 🟡 Fair — undersized for container | ➡️ | | Citronella | 🟡 Fair — needs pruning | ⬆️ | | Onions (4) | 🟠 Poor — wrong season | ↘️ | | Lavender | 🟠 Poor — half dying back | ↘️ | | Carrots | 💀 Dead | ✖️ | Transplant timing observations: Tomatoes and peppers should be 8–12" tall with first flowers by May 17 in Houston Zone 9a. Current measurements: 3–5" with no flowers. They're behind schedule — recoverable with weekly fish emulsion feedings and consistent water, but every week now is stolen from peak harvest window before the 90°F+ wall in mid-June kills fruit set on tomatoes. Mulch-on-stem issue across raised bed: On close inspection, straw mulch is piled too close to stems on several tomatoes and BP2. Houston humidity + mulch contact = stem rot risk and pest harborage. Universal fix: pull mulch back 2" from every stem. Onion wrong-season reality: Houston onions want October–January sowing for May–June harvest. April-sown onions in a Zone 9a summer don't bulb properly. The four current shoots will be harvested as scallions in 4–6 weeks, then the space reused. Proper onion sets (small bulbs) get planted in October — variety should be Texas Grano 1015Y (short-day, perfect for Houston). Lavender mixed performance: Two clumps flowering well, two clumps showing heavy dieback. Likely root rot from Houston humidity + possibly residual fertilizer salts. Treatment: aggressive prune back to silver/green wood, stop watering for a week, stop fertilizing entirely. Lavender is a 1–2 year crop in Houston regardless — consider replacing failing clumps with rosemary (same look, actually thrives here). Carrot bucket repurposing: The 5-gallon orange Home Depot bucket has good soil. Best replacement crops for late-May Houston planting: okra (single plant fills the bucket, loves heat), bush beans (60-day harvest), or a sweet potato slip (huge tuber yield). 🚨 Issues - Lime tree pest pressure — citrus leaf miner on new flush (cosmetic, tree outgrows it but reduces vigor) + slugs climbing at night. Treatment plan: weekly neem oil on new growth, iron phosphate bait (Sluggo) around pot base, copper tape barrier on pot rim, thin straw mulch around trunk. - Tomato/pepper growth lag —

title: Bell Pepper Care Log
body: 🫑 Bell Pepper Plants Variety: California Wonder Type: Annual fruiting vegetable (Solanaceae) Plant Count: 2 (BP1, BP2) Seeds Sown: 2026-04-14 (indoor nursery) Transplanted Outdoor: ~2026-05-10 to 2026-05-15 Location: Raised bed, against SW-facing house wall Mulch: Straw Support: Tomato-style cages installed (overkill for size, fine for now) --- Latest Observation — 2026-05-17 The two bell peppers are showing very different growth rates — one is well ahead of the other. - BP1 (foreground, Image 10): Strong, robust seedling with thick stem, ~4–5" tall, four glossy dark-green leaves, healthy waxy cuticle. This is the textbook ideal. - BP2 (background/Image 11): Noticeably smaller, ~3" tall, lighter green leaves, thinner stem. Likely under-developed at transplant or experiencing more shock. Health Status - BP1: 🟢 Excellent — best-looking transplant in the whole bed - BP2: 🟡 Fair — alive but lagging significantly Observations / Concerns - Both have straw mulch — appropriate distance from BP1's stem, slightly close on BP2 - No pest damage, no discoloration beyond the size difference - Blue plant label visible reading "Bell Pepper" - Peppers actually prefer the Houston heat more than tomatoes — these should accelerate once temps climb Recommended Actions Immediate: - [ ] Pull mulch back 1–2" from BP2's stem - [ ] Apply fish emulsion drench to both (2 tbsp/gallon) - [ ] If Myco Supreme wasn't applied at transplant, drench 1 tbsp/gallon around each root zone - [ ] Water deeply 1×/day, ~3/4 gallon per plant Within 2 weeks: - [ ] Pinch off first flower buds on both plants to encourage bushier growth - [ ] Begin weekly fish emulsion feedings - [ ] Plants do not need cages until they start setting fruit — current cages are fine Watch for: - Aphids on new growth (common in Houston May–June) - Sunscald on fruit once they start setting (the shade cloth plan helps here too) - Blossom drop above 90°F daytime / 75°F nighttime — peppers are more heat-tolerant than tomatoes but still drop flowers in extreme heat History | Date | Event | |------|-------| | 2026-04-14 | Seeds sown indoors on heat mat | | ~2026-05-05 | Hardening off begins | | ~2026-05-12 | Transplanted to raised bed with Myco Supreme | | 2026-05-17 | Health check — BP1 excellent, BP2 lagging |

title: Carrot Care Log (Memorial)
body: 🥕 Carrots — RIP Variety: Not specified Type: Cool-season biennial root vegetable Plant Count: 4 attempted — all dead as of 2026-05-17 Container: Orange 5-gallon bucket on patio Location: Near front door Status: 💀 ALL DECEASED --- Latest Observation — 2026-05-17 The orange bucket contains only soil, perlite, and a scattered layer of dry straw. No live carrot plants are visible. Surface is dry and undisturbed. Postmortem — Likely Causes of Death 1. Wrong season for Houston (most likely cause). Carrots are a cool-season crop. In Zone 9a they should be direct-sown September–February for winter/spring harvest. Sowing in April–May puts germination right into 85°F+ soil temperatures, which carrots refuse to germinate in. 2. Inconsistent moisture during germination. Carrot seeds need 14–21 days of constantly moist soil to germinate. A single dry-out kills the entire batch. Containers in Houston sun dry out in hours. 3. Container choice. A 5-gallon bucket is fine for depth (carrots need 10–12" loose soil), but the orange color absorbs heat, baking the root zone. Black or terra cotta is even worse — light-colored or fabric pots stay cooler. 4. Possible burial under mulch. Carrot seeds are tiny and must be sown only 1/4" deep. Heavy straw on top can prevent emergence entirely. Lessons Learned - ❌ Don't direct-sow carrots in Houston after February - ❌ Don't bury fine seeds under heavy mulch - ❌ Don't let container surface dry out during germination - ✅ Cover newly-sown seed with thin board or burlap to keep soil moist (remove on first emergence) - ✅ Use vermiculite (not straw) as a light cover layer for tiny seeds Recommended Recovery Plan The bucket and soil are still usable. Don't waste them. Option A — Repurpose for a heat-loving crop now: - Bush beans (60-day harvest, will handle Houston summer) - Okra (loves Houston heat, single plant will fill the bucket) - Sweet potato slip (huge tuber yield from one slip) Option B — Save for proper carrot timing: - Empty bucket, refresh soil with compost - Re-sow September 15 for late-fall/early-winter harvest - Use Nantes, Danvers, or Little Finger varieties (good for containers) History | Date | Event | |------|-------| | ~2026-04-15 | Carrot seeds direct-sown in orange bucket | | ~2026-05-01 | No emergence noted | | 2026-05-17 | Confirmed total failure — bucket empty |

title: Citronella Care Log
body: 🌿 Citronella Plant Variety: Pelargonium citrosum ("Citronella Mosquito Plant" / scented geranium) Type: Tender perennial (annual in cold climates, perennial in Houston) Plant Count: 1 Container: Brown plastic pot on herb station shelf Location: Herb pipe table, partial shade Mulch: Straw --- Latest Observation — 2026-05-17 The citronella has put on significant new growth at the top — fresh light-green frilly leaves on a single central stem reaching upward. The lower portion of the plant shows woody/dead stems and some brown crispy foliage, while new vegetation is concentrated at the apex. This is a classic recovery pattern — the plant lost older foliage to winter/transplant stress and is now regrowing from the top. Health Status 🟡 Fair → improving — new growth is healthy, lower plant needs cleanup Observations / Concerns - Dead/woody lower stems should be pruned to redirect energy to new growth - Plant label "Citronella Mosquito Plant" visible on the side - Straw mulch is heavy around the base — may be holding too much moisture against the crown - Note: True citronella oil comes from Cymbopogon nardus (a grass). This "citronella" geranium contains citronellol but is not nearly as effective at repelling mosquitoes as marketed. Still a nice patio plant. Recommended Actions Immediate: - [ ] Prune dead/woody lower stems with clean shears — cut back to where you see green growth - [ ] Pull straw mulch back ~3" from the crown — these plants prefer their crown exposed - [ ] Check pot drainage — lift pot and confirm water drains freely from bottom holes - [ ] Apply diluted fish emulsion (1 tbsp/gallon) — light feed once monthly Ongoing care: - [ ] Let soil dry between waterings — these are drought-tolerant once established - [ ] Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage bushier growth - [ ] Move to brighter location if possible — they like 6+ hours of sun Watch for: - Yellowing leaves → overwatering (most common issue) - White cottony patches on stems → mealybugs (wipe with rubbing alcohol on cotton swab) - Fungal leaf spots → cut affected leaves, improve airflow History | Date | Event | |------|-------| | Pre-2026 | Existing potted plant on herb station | | ~2026-04-01 | Myco Supreme drench applied | | 2026-05-10 | Yellowing lower leaves noted — drainage concern | | 2026-05-17 | Health check — new top growth strong, lower stems need pruning |

title: Corn Care Log
body: 🌽 Corn Variety: Not specified — confirm Type: Annual grain (Poaceae) Plant Count: 4 stalks Seeds Sown: ~2026-04-01 (transplanted outdoor earlier than other crops) Container: Large black plastic pot (~7–10 gallon) Location: Against house wall, near grass edge Mulch: Straw --- Latest Observation — 2026-05-17 The corn looks fantastic . Four healthy stalks are visible, each with broad green ribbon-like blades arching gracefully outward. Color is uniform vibrant green, no chlorosis or pest damage. Stalks are ~12–18" tall. Distinctive purple/red coloration at the base of stalks is normal for many sweet corn varieties — it's pigmentation expression, not stress. Health Status 🟢 Excellent — vigorous, well-established, on track Observations / Concerns - 4 stalks in one container is borderline crowded — corn needs cross-pollination from at least a 4×4 block ideally, but 4 in close proximity will partially work - Wind pollination is the main mechanism — gentle hand-shaking of tassels (when they form) helps ensure all ears get pollinated - Straw mulch looks great, no contact issues - Single-pot corn is unusual but workable as long as it's deep enough — looks like it is Recommended Actions Immediate: - [ ] Water deeply 1×/day during hot weather — corn is a thirsty crop - [ ] Top-dress with compost or apply fish emulsion (2 tbsp/gallon) weekly — corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder - [ ] Once stalks hit ~24" tall, side-dress with high-N organic fertilizer (blood meal, alfalfa meal) Pollination window (2–4 weeks out): - [ ] When tassels (male flowers at top) and silks (female, from emerging ears) appear, gently shake stalks daily to release pollen onto silks - [ ] Each silk strand connects to one kernel — incomplete pollination = gappy ears - [ ] Consider hand-collecting tassel pollen in a paper bag and brushing onto silks for full pollination Watch for: - Earworms (caterpillars at the tip of ears) — drop a few drops of vegetable oil into the silks once they brown - Wind damage — if stalks lean, hill up soil around bases for support - Aphids on tassels — usually self-resolves with ladybug predation Harvest - Sweet corn is ready when silks turn brown and dry, kernels are plump, and a punctured kernel releases milky liquid (not clear, not doughy) - Twist + pull down to harvest - Eat within hours of picking for peak sweetness (sugars convert to starch fast) History | Date | Event | |------|-------| | ~2026-03-25 | Seeds sown indoors | | ~2026-04-15 | Transplanted outdoor to large pot | | 2026-05-10 | Strong vigorous growth noted | | 2026-05-17 | Health check — excellent, ~12–18" tall, on track |

title: Lavender Care Log
body: 💜 Lavender Variety: Likely English lavender ( Lavandula angustifolia ) based on label Type: Mediterranean perennial herb Plant Count: 3–4 clumps in a rectangular planter Container: Long black rectangular planter on herb station upper shelf Location: Herb pipe table, partial-to-full sun Mulch: Wood chip / bark mulch (better than straw for lavender — drains well) --- Latest Observation — 2026-05-17 Mixed performance across the planter. Two clumps show good silvery-green foliage and have produced purple flower spikes (one prominent stalk in the photo). The other clumps are showing significant browning and dieback — dry crispy leaves, especially on the lower portions. The rightmost clump looks particularly stressed. Health Status 🟠 Poor to fair — half of the plants are stressed/dying, half are recovering and flowering Observations / Concerns - Lavender struggles in Houston. It's a Mediterranean plant that wants dry, alkaline, well-drained soil — Houston gives it humid, acidic, often waterlogged conditions. - The browning is consistent with either: 1. Root rot from too much moisture (most likely culprit in Houston) 2. Winter dieback that hasn't been pruned out yet 3. Salt buildup from synthetic fertilizers (Miracle-Gro?) - Good signs: New silvery growth on healthy clumps, flower production on at least 2 stems - Bark mulch is correct choice (much better than straw for lavender) Recommended Actions Immediate: - [ ] Prune aggressively — cut all brown/dead growth back to where you see green or silver wood. Don't cut into bare brown wood (it won't resprout). - [ ] Check planter drainage — if water pools, drill more holes or add more grit/sand to soil - [ ] Stop fertilizing entirely — lavender hates rich soil. Fertilizer is making it worse. - [ ] Water only when soil is bone dry 3" down — much less than other plants Ongoing: - [ ] Apply a top-dressing of crushed oyster shell or garden lime to raise pH (lavender prefers alkaline 6.5–7.5) - [ ] Add coarse builder's sand or perlite to topsoil to improve drainage further - [ ] After flowering ends, prune flowers off + give plants a "haircut" to encourage bushy growth Houston-specific reality check: - Most lavender varieties last 1–2 years in Houston before declining - Lavandula x intermedia "Provence" and L. dentata (French lavender) handle humidity better than English - Consider replacing failing clumps with rosemary — same look, same care, but actually thrives in Houston Watch for - Spittlebugs (foamy spit on stems) — rinse off with hose - Fungal stem rot at base — pull affected plants immediately to save the others - Spider mites in dry weather — strong water spray on leaves History | Date | Event | |------|-------| | Pre-2026 | Existing planted clumps on herb station | | ~2026-04-01 | Myco Supreme drench applied to surviving plants | | 2026-05-10 | Some flowering noted, some clumps stressed | | 2026-05-17 | Health check — significant dieback on half, others flowering |

title: Lime Tree Care Log
body: 🍋 Lime Tree Variety: Persian or Kaffir lime (confirm — leaves are single-blade, suggesting Persian; Kaffir has distinctive double-lobed leaves) Type: Tropical citrus tree (perennial) Plant Count: 1 Container: Large black plastic pot (~10 gallon) Location: Patio, partial sun against house wall Mulch: Straw --- Latest Observation — 2026-05-17 The lime tree is thriving . Dense, glossy dark-green foliage forms a full canopy with vigorous upward growth and good lateral branching. Fresh light-green new growth visible at the apex indicates active flushing. Visible issues: - Slime/shine on leaves — some surface glossiness consistent with slug or snail trails (Matt's direct observation) - Leaf cupping and curling on multiple branches — distinct from slug damage, classic citrus leaf miner pattern (larvae tunnel inside leaf, visible as silvery squiggly lines, leaves curl protectively) - A few leaves show edge browning / tip burn — could be salt buildup or under-watering history Health Status 🟢 Excellent — but actively under pest pressure Pest Diagnosis Likely two concurrent issues : 1. Citrus leaf miner ( Phyllocnistis citrella ) — endemic in Houston, attacks new flush growth, causes the cupped/curled leaves and silver tunnel patterns. The tree outgrows this; cosmetic damage only. 2. Slugs or snails — surface slime on lower leaves. They climb up trunks at night, especially when straw mulch stays damp. Recommended Actions Slug/snail control: - [ ] Apply iron phosphate bait (Sluggo, Garden Safe brand) sprinkled around pot base — safe for pets/wildlife - [ ] Wrap pot rim with copper tape as a barrier - [ ] Alternative/supplement: shallow dish of beer at ground level overnight - [ ] Confirm with flashlight check at dusk - [ ] Pull straw mulch back from the trunk and thin out the layer — slugs love damp dense mulch Citrus leaf miner control: - [ ] Spray neem oil weekly (1 tbsp per gallon water + a drop of dish soap to emulsify) during new growth flush periods only - [ ] Time sprays for evening when bees aren't active - [ ] Don't remove damaged leaves — the tree still photosynthesizes through them - [ ] Repeat for next flush in summer General citrus care: - [ ] Apply Espoma Citrus-tone (or similar citrus-specific fertilizer) monthly Mar–Oct - [ ] Deep water weekly — let top 2" dry between waterings - [ ] Plan a 15–20 gallon pot upgrade within the next year as the tree fills the current pot - [ ] Strong hose spray every few days to disrupt pest egg-laying and dislodge crawlers Watch for - Citrus rust mite (bronzed fruit later in season) - Asian citrus psyllid (vector for citrus greening disease, devastating if present) — small mottled-wing insects on new growth - Yellowing leaves with green veins → micronutrient deficiency (zinc, iron, manganese) — citrus-specific fertilizer addresses this - Flower buds → confirm pollination History | Date | Event | |------|-------| | Pre-2026 | Established potted citrus on patio | | ~2026-04-01 | Myco Supreme drench applied | | 2026-05-10 | Thriving — flower buds forming | | 2026-05-17 | Health check — vigorous growth, leaf miner damage + slug slime observed | Care Notes - Watering: Deep weekly soaking, let top 2" dry between waterings - Light: Full sun, 8+ hours - Feeding: Citrus-tone or fish + kelp emulsion monthly Mar–Oct - Pruning: Light pruning after fruit harvest; remove suckers from below graft union - Cold protection: Sensitive below 40°F — move under cover or wrap during Houston winter cold snaps

title: Onion Care Log
body: 🧅 Onion Plants Variety: Evergreen Bunching (or Sweet Spanish — confirm label) Type: Biennial bulb / perennial bunching Plant Count: 4 (O1, O2, O3, O4) Seeds Sown: Unclear — direct sown or transplanted recently Location: Raised bed, tucked between larger plants Mulch: Straw --- Latest Observation — 2026-05-17 All four onion shoots are present but significantly under-developed . Each appears as a single or paired thin grass-like green shoot ~2–4" tall, weak and floppy, lying nearly horizontal in some cases. - O1 (Image 12): Barely visible single shoot, very weak - O2 (Image 13): Two shoots curving outward, ~3" long, alive but spindly - O3 (Image 14): Single curled shoot near "Onion" white label - O4 (Image 15): Single thin shoot Health Status 🟠 Poor — alive but growth is well behind schedule Observations / Concerns - Wrong season for Houston: Onions in Zone 9a should be started in Oct–Jan for May–June harvest. Starting now means they'll struggle through summer heat and may bolt without forming bulbs. - All shoots are weak/spindly — indicates either too-low light at germination, overcrowded planting cells, or weak seed - Excessive straw mulch around onions can smother them — these need exposed soil and full sun on the tops - The plant labels mention they should be at the edges of the raised bed to avoid competition Recommended Actions Immediate: - [ ] Pull straw mulch completely off the onion crowns — they need light on their green tops - [ ] Don't expect bulb formation this round; treat as a green-onion / scallion crop - [ ] Harvest as scallions when shoots reach 6–8" — pull whole plant or snip greens - [ ] Plant new onion sets (small bulbs from nursery) in October for proper spring 2027 harvest Strategy decision: - Option A — Let them grow as scallions, harvest in 4–6 weeks, then replant the space with a heat-tolerant crop (basil, okra, or okra seedlings) - Option B — Pull them now and use the space for something more productive History | Date | Event | |------|-------| | 2026-04-14 (est) | Seeds sown indoors | | ~2026-05-10 | Transplanted to raised bed edges | | 2026-05-17 | Health check — under-developed, treat as scallions | Notes for Future Seasons - Houston onion calendar: Start seeds late October, transplant in December–January, harvest May–June - Alternative: Buy onion sets (small bulbs) in January for faster spring crop - Sweet Spanish needs longer day length than Houston provides; switch to short-day varieties like Texas Grano 1015Y (the legendary "Texas sweet")

title: Potato Tower Care Log
body: 🥔 Potato Tower Variety: Seed potato (variety not recorded — confirm if known) Type: Annual tuber crop (Solanaceae) Container: White plastic clothes hamper with oval ventilation holes System: Layered soil/hay vertical grow — add layers as plants grow taller Started: Early April 2026 (estimated) --- Latest Observation — 2026-05-17 The potato tower is the star of the outdoor garden right now. title: Patio Orientation
body: The patio house wall faces 230° (southwest) . This is the toughest orientation for Houston gardening. Implications and mitigations for Outdoor Garden Layout and Garden Monitor. What 230° Means - No morning sun — the house blocks east light from the patio. - Full-blast afternoon sun — from roughly noon through sunset. The hottest, most intense window of the day in Houston. - Wall radiates absorbed heat — the house wall acts as a thermal mass, soaking sun all afternoon and re-emitting heat onto the plants long after the sun moves off. - Microclimate is hotter than ambient — soil surface in the raised bed could hit 130°F+ in July/August without mulch. Even ambient air against the wall sits 5–10°F above the local forecast. Per-Crop Heat Tolerance | Crop | Tolerance | What happens at this orientation | |---|---|---| | 🍅 Tomato (Beefsteak) | Drops flowers and stops setting fruit above 95°F. | Spring harvest May–June, then production pause June–September until nights cool. Fall production resumes late September. | | 🌶️ Bell Pepper, Jalapeño | More heat-tolerant than tomato. | Produce through summer with watering discipline. Jalapeños actually thrive. | | 🍉 Watermelon | Loves heat IF watered consistently. | Will keep producing all summer; needs daily watering. | | 🌽 Corn | Moderate. | Has the wind/grass area; gets more balanced sun than the wall plants. | | 💜 Lavender | Mediterranean — wants heat + dry. | Thrives. The hot wall actually suits it. | | 🌿 Spearmint | Wilts in afternoon sun. | Already showing stress — needs partial shade or relocation. | | 🍋 Lime tree | Heat-loving. | Thrives. | | 🥗 Lettuce / Cilantro | Bolts above 80°F. | Don't even try outdoors here past April. Indoor / hydroponic only. | Mitigations 1. Straw mulch everywhere (already applied) Already in place across raised bed, corn containers, herbs. Drops surface soil temp 15–20°F. Single highest-impact thing in Houston gardening. Pull mulch ~1" away from each stem to prevent rot. 2. Morning watering only Plants need to be hydrated before the afternoon assault hits. Evening watering = wet foliage overnight + Houston humidity → fungal pressure (powdery mildew, black spot). Water at the base, never on leaves. See Watering Guide for per-plant schedules. 3. Shade cloth (deploy late May) Get 40–50% shade cloth (white or aluminet/reflective silver). Drape over the raised bed during peak afternoon hours (~1 PM to 5 PM). Drops effective temp 10–15°F — the difference between tomatoes producing and shutting down. Don't go higher than 50% shade — plants still need light to fruit. Don't deploy before late May either — early-season plants want all the sun they can get to establish strong root systems. See Shade Strategy for the PVC frame design. 4. Plant placement within the bed - Tomatoes at the east end of the raised bed — they catch the least direct wall-radiated heat (the east end is furthest from peak afternoon sun angle on a 230° wall). - Peppers/jalapeños in the middle — they handle the hottest zone best. - Onions tucked between — short, doesn't compete for vertical space, cool roots from neighbor shade. 5. Spearmint relocation Mint is the plant most stressed by this orientation. Options: - Move to a partial-shade spot if any exists (e.g., east side of the house if accessible). - Upsize the pot and water more frequently. - Accept the seasonal hit — mint often goes "summer dormant" in Houston and rebounds in fall. 6. Container-level heat management Dark plastic containers (corn, watermelon) absorb a lot of solar. Mulch on top of the soil drops surface temps; consider also wrapping the outside of the container in light-colored fabric or shade cloth for the worst heat weeks if leaves start curling. 7. Future: temperature-driven automation Once Garden Monitor is wired up, Arduino Nicla Sense Env + DHT22 sensors at each zone log to InfluxDB on the Raspberry Pi 5. Rules to deploy: - Delay watering past 6 PM if ambient 100°F (avoid evening leaf-wetness). - Auto-trigger sha

title: Shade Strategy
body: Shade cloth design for the raised bed in Outdoor Garden Layout — protection from late-May through mid-September Houston afternoon heat. Critical given the Patio Orientation. Why You Need It Tomatoes drop flowers + stop setting fruit above 95°F. The southwest-facing patio wall pushes the raised bed's effective temperature 5–15°F above ambient most afternoons June–September. Shade cloth restores tomato production through summer. Without shade cloth on a 230°-facing bed, expect: - Tomato production pause: June through September. - Pepper / jalapeño: still produce but stressed. - Soil surface temps at the bed: 130°F+ in peak afternoon (mulch keeps the root zone livable, but leaves get cooked). With 40–50% shade cloth deployed afternoon hours (1–5 PM): - Effective temp drops 10–15°F. - Tomato production continues into July. - Less leaf burn across all crops. Specs | Item | Spec | Why | |---|---|---| | Shade rating | 40–50% | Balance — enough shade to drop temp, enough light to fruit. 50% blocks too much light; <40% doesn't drop temp enough. | | Color | White or aluminet (reflective silver) | Reflects heat instead of absorbing. Avoid black — gets hot itself. | | Frame material | 1" PVC pipe + tee fittings | Cheap, lightweight, reusable, no glue (so it disassembles seasonally). | | Vertical pipe height | ~5 ft | Above the bed wall, allows 6 ft tomato growth underneath. | | Crossbar length | ~8 ft (matches bed length) | Spans the long edge of the raised bed. | Frame Design Verticals: Two 5-ft 1" PVC pipes at the back corners of the raised bed (against the wall side). Crossbar: One 8-ft 1" PVC pipe across the top, joined to the verticals with tee fittings (no glue). Anchoring: Either (a) clamp the verticals to the bed walls with large hose clamps or U-bolts, or (b) sink them 8–10" into the soil inside the bed at each end — bed wall provides lateral support. Cloth attachment: Eye hooks on the house wall above the window for the rear of the cloth. Binder clips or zip ties to the front of the crossbar. Cloth drapes from wall down over the crossbar and angles forward like an awning. Bottom open: Don't enclose — air must flow underneath, otherwise it becomes an oven. Materials List | Item | Source | Approx. cost | |---|---|---| | 1" PVC pipe (10 ft) × 2 | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$8–10 | | 1" PVC tee fittings × 2 | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$3 | | 1" PVC end caps × 2 (optional) | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$2 | | Hose clamps (large) × 4 OR U-bolts × 4 | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$5 | | Eye hooks × 2 | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$2 | | 6 × 8 ft (or 6 × 10 ft) shade cloth panel, 40–50%, white/aluminet | Amazon (search "shade cloth 50% white 6x8") | ~$15–25 | | Binder clips (jumbo, 8-pack) | Already on hand or ~$3 | | | Zip ties (variety pack) | Already on hand or ~$3 | | Total: ~$35–45. Timing | Date | Action | |---|---| | Early–Mid May | Don't deploy yet. Plants want full sun while establishing. | | Late May / Early June | Deploy when daily highs consistently hit 95°F+ . | | June – September | Keep deployed during peak afternoon (~1–5 PM). Can leave up 24/7 — Houston nights stay warm enough that morning sun still gets through the cloth's diffused light. | | Late September | Remove when daily highs drop below 90°F. Tomatoes resume fruit set. | Daily Operation (Manual) Two options: 1. Deploy once, leave up all summer. Simplest. The 40–50% rating still allows enough light through morning + diffused light, and the angle puts most blockage on afternoon sun. 2. Deploy/retract daily. Higher labor but maximum morning sun. Pull cloth back at 5–6 PM, redeploy at noon. Cloth folds into a small bundle; takes 30 seconds. For most of summer, option 1 is the right tradeoff. Why NOT a Pop-Up Canopy A pop-up shade canopy (tailgate-style) would be easier to deploy, BUT: - Houston thunderstorms blow them away (lost canopies = ~$60 each + plant damage if it falls). - Not anchored to the structure. - Hard to angle correctly for a SW-facing wall. The PVC frame is sturdier, ancho

title: Outdoor Garden Layout
body: Patio garden design for Garden Monitor — raised bed, corn containers, watermelon trellis, herb stand, lime tree, and potato tower. Houston stone patio, southwest-facing house wall. Site - Stone patio against the house wall. Wall faces 230° (southwest) — see Patio Orientation for the heat-management implications. - Hose spigot accessible at one end of the patio (future drip irrigation tap point). - Raised bed sits on stone, not soil — drainage layer matters. Layout Map Raised Bed (8' × 2' × 16–18" deep, galvanized steel) Already built and placed against the house wall. Mulched with straw, ready for transplants. Plant placements (best 2 of each variety, transplanted at 4–6 true leaves): - 2 × Tomato (Beefsteak) — 24" apart, with cage or stake each. Place at the east end where they'll catch the least afternoon-wall heat. - 2 × Bell Pepper (CA Wonder) — 18" apart, middle. - 2 × Jalapeño (Gigante) — 18" apart, middle near peppers (same family, similar needs). - 8 × Onion (Evergreen Bunching) — tucked between the larger plants (tiny footprint). - Basil — between tomatoes (companion plant; supposedly improves flavor + repels some pests). - ~~Broccoli~~ — Houston summer kills heading. Save seedlings for fall replant. Planting hole protocol: 1 Tbsp Trifecta Myco Supreme into each hole. Set root ball on top, backfill. Don't combine with Miracle-Gro synthetic fertilizer (kills the fungi). Use compost tea or fish emulsion instead. Why this layout: - 2 ft wide max — reachable from the front (back is against the wall). - 12" minimum depth required for tomato/pepper roots; 16–18" is even better in Houston summer when shallow soil cooks. - Landscape fabric on the bottom of the bed before filling — prevents soil washing through onto the patio while still allowing drainage. Add 15% for settling = ~18 cu ft. | Bag size | bags | |---|---| | 2 cu ft (standard) | 8–10 | | 1.5 cu ft | 11–12 | Cost-saving mix recipe (instead of all premium potting): - 40% topsoil (cheap, ~$3/bag) - 40% compost (~$5/bag) - 20% perlite (~$5/bag) → Total ~$40–60 vs $70–130 for all-premium. Existing Miracle-Gro can fill in as part of the compost portion (just not in spots that will get Myco Supreme later). Corn Containers Two large circular planters (~18–20" diameter) sitting on grass off the patio. - 5 stalks per container in a cross pattern — 1 in center, 4 around at ~8" from center. - 10 plants total across both pots — tight for wind pollination but workable since the containers are touching each other. - When tassels appear, shake them gently each morning to drop pollen onto silks below. - Mulch with 2–3 inches of straw , leaving a 1" gap around each stalk (no stem rot). Why not the raised bed: watermelon is one of the heaviest feeders + drinkers in gardening. Roots spread 2–3 ft wide; would invade tomato/pepper space within weeks and stress everything. body: Status snapshot of the indoor seed-starting nursery for Garden Monitor. Seeds planted 2026-04-14 , four trays of 12 cells each on the Nursery System Design. Garage location, Houston. Shelf-by-Shelf Layout | Shelf | Tray | Contents | |---|---|---| | Shelf 4 (top) | Big container (12 cells) + egg carton | 2 bell pepper, 2 jalapeño, 2 tomato, 4 onion · egg carton: assorted peppers/tomatoes/jalapeños in eggshell halves | | Shelf 3 | 12-cell tray | Bell pepper, tomato, onion (4 each) | | Shelf 2 left | 12-cell tray | Corn (Golden Bantam), broccoli (Waltham), carrot (Scarlet Nantes) | | Shelf 2 right | 12-cell tray | Oregano, rosemary, watermelon | | Shelf 1 (bottom) | 12-cell tray | Three lettuce varieties: Buttercrunch Butterhead, Ruby Red, Black Seeded Simpson | Layout is intentional: heat rises inside the PVC cover, so warm-season crops (peppers, tomatoes, jalapeños) sit on the upper shelves and lettuce stays at the bottom where it's coolest. Natural temperature gradient = no second heat mat needed. 📸 Photo placeholder — overall shelf view, day 7 (2026-04-21) Germination Status (Day 5–10) | Status | Items | |---|---| | ✅ Growing well | Corn (star — 4–5" → 8–10" by day 10), watermelon, broccoli, onion, single tomato | | 🟡 Just starting | A few lettuce sprouts (Black Seeded Simpson, Ruby Red), bell pepper sprout | | 🔴 No signs after 10+ days | Top shelf big container + egg carton (likely heat-killed — see below) | | ⏳ Normal — still in window | Carrot (10–14 days), oregano (7–14), rosemary (14–21) | ⚠️ Heat Issue — Resolved The garage greenhouse hit 37°C / 98.6°F at the top shelf during peak afternoon — caused by Houston ambient + grow lights + sealed PVC cover. Lettuce went thermodormant; top-shelf seeds likely got cooked. Temperature timeline: | Reading | Conditions | What it means | |---|---|---| | 37.0°C / 98.6°F | Top shelf, afternoon, cover closed | Too hot for everything — even peppers stress at 95°F+ | | 33.3°C / 91.9°F | Bottom shelf, afternoon, covers off | Still too hot for lettuce (thermodormancy 75°F) | | 25.2°C / 77.4°F | Bottom shelf, 7:20 AM, covers off, 70% RH | Workable for most crops; borderline for lettuce | Mitigations applied: - PVC cover fully off during the day , only on at night if garage drops below 65°F. - Box fan pointed at shelves for airflow — drops effective temp 5–10°F. - Hygrometer moved to bottom shelf to track lettuce zone. - Top-shelf big container declared dead — focus shifted to the strong Shelf 3 tray. 📸 Photo placeholder — hygrometer reading (37°C / 98.6°F), then 25.2°C morning reading Eggshell Planters Note Many top-shelf cells use eggshell halves with cracked tops sitting in a cardboard egg carton. The shells are essentially mini sealed pots — moisture stays in much longer than bare cardboard. Adjustments: - Reduce misting to once daily (vs twice for plastic cells). - 1–2 teaspoons max per shell per misting — eggshells don't drain. - Poke a pin hole in the bottom of each shell for drainage and to enable bottom-watering from the carton. - Bonus at transplant: crack the shell more around the sides and plant the whole thing . Eggshell decomposes and releases calcium carbonate → prevents tomato blossom-end rot. Watering Schedule See Watering Guide for the full per-shelf rules. Quick version: cells should feel like a wrung-out sponge (damp throughout, never wet). Water daily on Shelf 4 (driest), every 1–2 days on Shelves 1–3, twice daily on the egg carton. Myco Supreme Don't apply yet. Mycorrhizal fungi need active root contact to colonize. Hold until transplant day for tomatoes, peppers, jalapeños, watermelon, corn — sprinkle 1 Tbsp into each planting hole. Outdoor lavender/citronella/spearmint can get a dose now (already-established root systems). See Transplant Timeline for dates. What's Working / Not Working Working: - Tier strategy — heat-loving crops up top, lettuce on bottom = natural temp zoning. - Shelf 3 tray (peppers/tomatoes/onions) is the breakout success. - Eggshell technique

title: Transplant Timeline
body: Per-plant readiness criteria and target dates for moving seedlings from the Indoor Nursery to the Outdoor Garden Layout. Updated as the Garden Monitor nursery progresses. The Rule A seedling is ready to transplant when it has 4–6 true leaves AND the stem is thick enough to support upright growth. Cell-bound (roots circling the bottom) means overdue . Current Status — Day 12 since 2026-04-14 planting | Plant | Source tray | Days to ready | Target date | Status | |---|---|---|---|---| | Corn (Golden Bantam) | Shelf 2 left | OVERDUE — roots cell-bound | Today (transplant immediately) | 🚨 | | Watermelon | Shelf 2 right | ~3–7 days | Within 10 days | 🟡 — leggy, needs stem mounding now | | Tomato (Beefsteak) | Shelf 3 | 14–21 days | ~2 weeks | ⏳ — wait for 4–6 true leaves | | Bell Pepper | Shelf 3 | 14–21 days | ~2 weeks | ⏳ | | Jalapeño Gigante | Shelf 3 (+ duplicates lost on Shelf 4) | 14–21 days | ~2 weeks | ⏳ | | Onion (Evergreen Bunching) | Shelf 3 | 7–14 days | 1–2 weeks | 🟡 | | Broccoli | Shelf 2 left | N/A — Houston summer kills heading | Hold for fall replant in August | ⏸️ | | Carrot | Shelf 2 left | N/A — taproot doesn't transplant | Direct sow outdoors instead | ⏸️ | | Oregano | Shelf 2 right | 21–28 days | ~3–4 weeks | ⏳ | | Rosemary | Shelf 2 right | 28–35 days | ~4–5 weeks | ⏳ — slowest grower | | Lettuce (3 varieties) | Shelf 1 | N/A this season — bolts in heat | Hydroponics or fall replant | ⏸️ | Watermelon — Stem Mounding Fix The watermelon stems got leggy (too thin to support seed leaves; some fell over). Cause: light wasn't close enough during the high-heat days. Fix: - Mound soil up around fallen stems , burying partway up to just below the seed leaves. - Watermelon (like tomatoes) grows roots from buried stem — this actually helps long-term root mass. - Lower the grow light to 2–3 inches above the tallest plant on that shelf. - Real solution: get them outdoors. Sun is 5–10× more intense than grow lights and builds stronger stems naturally. Hardening-Off Checklist Don't take seedlings from indoor nursery to direct outdoor sun in one move — they'll sunburn and shock. Instead, harden off over 5–7 days : - [ ] Day 1: 1 hour outdoors in shade. - [ ] Day 2: 2 hours outdoors, partial shade. - [ ] Day 3: 3–4 hours outdoors, partial sun (morning OK). - [ ] Day 4: Half day outdoors, including some direct sun. - [ ] Day 5: Full day outdoors, dappled sun. Bring in for night. - [ ] Day 6: Full day + leave out overnight if temps stay above 60°F. - [ ] Day 7: Transplant. ⚠️ Skip hardening only if seedlings have already been exposed to high heat in the nursery (Houston garage heat counts) AND the transplant date has cooler weather forecast. Transplant-Day Protocol (per plant) 1. Water the seedling tray an hour before — easier extraction, less root damage. 2. Dig the planting hole to the depth of the cell + 1" extra. For tomatoes/peppers/jalapeños: dig deeper and bury part of the stem (they grow extra roots from buried stem = stronger plant). 3. Drop in 1 Tbsp Trifecta Myco Supreme at the bottom of the hole. 4. Pop the cell out gently. If roots are circling the bottom, loosen them with fingers or a chopstick. 5. Set the root ball on top of the Myco — roots in direct contact with the inoculant. 6. Backfill with soil , firming around the base. Don't pack too hard. 7. Water deeply — soak until water runs out the bottom. 8. Mulch with 2–3" straw, keeping a 1" gap around the stem. 9. For tomatoes, peppers, jalapeños: stake or cage immediately. Don't wait until they need it — driving stakes later damages roots. 10. For corn: plant in the cross pattern (1 center + 4 around at 8" from center) per Outdoor Garden Layout. Two containers touching each other for cross-pollination. 11. For watermelon: single vine in the 15–20 gal container by the trellis. Train the main vine up the trellis as it grows (loose ties). 12. title: Watering Guide
body: Per-plant watering schedules for the Garden Monitor indoor nursery and outdoor garden. Houston (Zone 9a, southwest-facing patio). The Universal Rule Soil should feel like a wrung-out sponge — damp throughout but never sitting in water. Stick your finger ¼" into the soil. If it feels dry, water. If it's still moist, leave it alone. Indoor Nursery — Seedling Stage | Tray / Location | Frequency | Method | Volume | |---|---|---|---| | Plastic cells (Shelves 1–3) | Every 1–2 days | Spray bottle / gentle mist | 1–2 Tbsp per cell, until surface evenly damp | | Big container (Shelf 4) | Every 1–2 days, water when top ¼" dry | Mist or gentle pour | More volume, deeper soak | | Egg carton (Shelf 4) — eggshell halves | Once daily (sealed eggshells retain moisture) | Mist | 1–2 tsp max per shell — easy to overwater | | Cardboard egg carton without shells | Twice daily (cardboard wicks fast) | Mist | Just enough to dampen cardboard visibly | When True Leaves Appear (~Week 2–3) Switch to bottom watering : - Pour water into the black catch tray. - Let cells wick moisture from below for ~20 min. - Dump any standing water afterward. - Encourages roots to grow downward + prevents damping-off (fungal seedling killer). Don't Do - ❌ Pour water directly onto seeds or tiny sprouts (dislodges them, compacts soil). - ❌ Leave standing water in catch trays 30 min (root rot, damping-off). - ❌ Mist top of eggshells if water pools and doesn't absorb in 1 minute (overwatering — shells don't drain). - ✅ Tip: Pin a tiny hole in the bottom of each eggshell for drainage. Heat Adjustments Warm shelves (3–4) dry faster than the cool bottom (lettuce). PVC cover helps retain humidity. Crack open the cover for 30 min daily for air circulation — prevents mold without dropping humidity too far. Outdoor — Per Plant Raised Bed (Pre-Transplant) - Frequency: Every 2–3 days while empty (just keep soil moist for transplant readiness). - Mulch covers everything; pull aside at planting spots when transplant day comes. Tomatoes (Raised Bed) — Once Transplanted - Frequency: Deep soak every 2–3 days; daily during establishment week. - Method: At the base, never on leaves (Houston humidity + wet foliage = fungal disaster). - Time: Morning only. Evening watering leaves wet leaves overnight. - Volume: Until water runs out the bottom of the bed. Shallow watering = shallow roots = stressed plants in summer. Peppers + Jalapeños (Raised Bed) - Same as tomatoes; slightly more drought-tolerant. Every 3 days fine in mild weather; daily in 95°F+ stretches. Onions (Raised Bed) - 1–2× per week. Don't overwater — onions rot in soggy soil. Surface dries between waterings is fine. Basil (Raised Bed) - More frequent than tomatoes; basil wilts visibly when thirsty. Every 1–2 days. Recovers fast after a soak. Corn (Circular Containers) - Establishment week (post-transplant): Deep soak every morning. Until water runs out the bottom drain holes. - Established (~week 2+): Stick finger 2" into soil under the straw. If dry at that depth, water. Daily in May/June heat. - At tasseling: Don't let it dry out — pollination is moisture-sensitive. - Time: Morning only. Watermelon (Container with Trellis) - Establishment week: Deep daily watering. - Established: Stick finger 2" deep under straw. Likely daily, sometimes twice daily above 95°F. Watermelon is 92% water by weight — needs constant supply for fruit. - At fruit set: Keep watering consistent . Erratic watering causes cracking + hollow heart. - One week before harvest: Reduce to every other day. Slight stress concentrates sugars = sweeter fruit. - Method: Base only, slow trickle under the straw. - Time: Morning only. - Harvest signs: Tendril nearest the fruit turns brown; belly spot turns from white to yellow. Lavender Box (Existing Herb Stand) - Frequency: Once a week max once established. Drier the better. - Method: Base only — wet foliage in Houston humidity = black leaves and death. - Cooldown: Minimum 4–5 days between waterings — enforced in Outdo

title: Nursery System Design
body: Indoor seed-starting nursery for Garden Monitor — drip irrigation, sensor wiring, camera, and tier strategy for the SOLIGT 5-tier greenhouse on the Raspberry Pi 5 / older Pi node. Hardware (Owned + Purchased) - SOLIGT 5-tier greenhouse — 63" tall, includes lights, timer, hygrometer, PVC cover. All-in-one nursery shelf. - Trifecta Myco Supreme — mycorrhizal fungi for transplant. - Miracle-Gro potting soil — but don't combine with Myco Supreme (high phosphorus kills the beneficial fungi). - 2 × Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor (Gikfun, already on hand). Components to Add (~$50–70) | Item | Search term | Approx. cost | |---|---|---| | 12V DC submersible pump (240 L/H, 3m head) | SIPYTOPF DC 12V submersible pump 240L/H 3M head | ~$7 | | 12V 2A DC power adapter | | ~$9 | | Adjustable drip emitters (50-pack) | MIXC 50pcs drip emitters fan stake 1/4 inch | ~$8 | | ADS1115 16-bit I2C ADC | HiLetgo ADS1115 16 bit I2C | ~$6 | | 5-pack Gikfun capacitive moisture sensors | (same brand as already owned) | ~$8 | | 4-channel relay module | | ~$6 | | DHT22 temp/humidity sensor | | ~$6 | | Jumper wires kit | | ~$7 | | Pi Camera Module (OV5647 IR-Cut, 5 MP) | Aokin Raspberry Pi camera IR-Cut OV5647 5MP | ~$12 | Total nursery system investment: ~$310–340 all-in including the SOLIGT shelf. 1. Pump Sizing The shelf is 63" tall (~5.3 ft). Pump must push water from a floor reservoir up to the top tier. - Head height is the key spec — get a pump rated for 6–10 ft of head for comfortable margin. - Flow rate matters less here — drip, not flood. 80–120 GPH at 5 ft head is plenty. - 12V DC submersible is preferred over USB — switchable via relay from the nursery Pi's GPIO for Garden Monitor automation integration. 2. Plumbing Layout - ½" main tubing (50 ft kit) runs vertically up the back of the shelf. - ½" elbow fittings (La Farah) turn the line horizontal at each tier. - ½"-to-¼" barbed tees (Kalolary) tap off at each tray position. - ¼" distribution tubing (Hourleey 50 ft) goes from each tee to a drip stake. - Adjustable drip emitters (~$8 / 50-pack) at the end of each ¼" line — dial flow per tray. Lettuce needs less than peppers. - End cap the ½" main line at the top (or fold-and-clamp). - PVC liners that come with the shelf catch drainage on each tier; can drip back down to the reservoir (closed loop) or into separate trays. 3. Moisture Sensor Architecture - Older Raspberry Pis have no analog input — capacitive sensors are analog, so we need an ADS1115 16-bit ADC over I2C . - ADS1115 gives 4 analog channels — enough for one sensor per tier on tiers 1–4. Tier 5 either shares with tier 4 or daisy-chains a second ADS1115. - Each sensor pushes into the soil of a representative tray on its tier. - Pi reads moisture every 30 seconds via I2C, publishes to MQTT topics like garden/nursery/tier1/moisture . - Hub evaluates threshold; pump relay fires for 10–15 seconds (calibrate from there). - Phase 2 upgrade: Add a small solenoid valve on each tier's ½" branch line, individually relay-controlled. Then we can water tier 3 (peppers) without watering tier 1 (lettuce that's already moist). 4. Camera Integration - Pi Camera Module (OV5647) mounted on the top tier looking down — captures tiers 1–3 from above. - Connects via CSI ribbon cable directly to the nursery Pi. - Schedule: capture every 4–6 hours. Generate timelapse via raspistill / libcamera . - One camera can't see all 5 tiers usefully — for full coverage, add a second on the bottom tier looking up, or build a motorized vertical slide rail (fun future project with a stepper + Arduino). - The Arduino Nicla Vision is better used outdoors where its edge ML and standalone WiFi shine. 5. Tier Layout Strategy Heat rises naturally inside the PVC enclosure — exploit this for free temperature zoning instead of buying a second heat mat: | Tier | Temp zone | Best for | |---|---|---| | Top (5/4) | Warmest (75–85°F) | Tomatoes, peppers, jalapeños, basil, watermelon | | Middle (3/2) | Moderate | Onions, oregano, rosemary

title: Houston Planting Calendar
body: Zone 9a (Houston, TX) seed-by-seed planting decisions for the Garden Monitor system. Last frost mid-February; March is the most valuable planting window of the year. Plant RIGHT NOW (Direct Seed Outdoors) - Okra (Clemson Spineless) — Houston's #1 summer crop. 1" deep, 12–18" apart. Soak seeds overnight first. Harvest in 55–65 days, produces straight through October. - Cucumber — 1" deep, 36" apart (sprawls). Trellis or cage saves space. Inconsistent moisture causes bitter fruit. Harvest 50–70 days. - Corn (Sweet) — Direct seed when soil temp hits 60°F. Plant in 4×4 blocks minimum (wind-pollinated). 1" deep, 10–12" apart. Not practical container-only. - Watermelon / Cantaloupe — Hill mounds, 2–3 seeds per hill, 1" deep. 6–8 ft per vine sprawl. Compact varieties for containers. 80–90 days to fruit. - Basil (Genovese & Lemon) — Barely cover seeds (need light to germinate). 12" apart. Pinch flower buds for season-long leaf production. Start Seeds Indoors NOW (Transplant in 3–4 Weeks) - Tomato — Heat mat 70–80°F, ¼" deep. 6–8 weeks to transplant size. Mid-May transplant is workable but tight before summer heat. For spring tomatoes from store transplants instead, plant the seeds for fall (transplant in July). - Pepper / Jalapeño Gigante — Same as tomato. 75–85°F soil. More heat-tolerant than tomatoes; produces well into Houston fall. - Rosemary — Slow germinator (14–21 days). 70°F soil. Perennial in Houston once established. Excellent drainage required — hates wet feet. Plant Now But Manage Expectations - Lettuce (Little Gem & Gourmet Blend) — Tail end of season. Will bolt mid-April–May. Better as a hydroponics crop or fall replant in September. Indoor in cool zone for now. - Cilantro — Bolts fast at 80°F+. Maybe 3–4 weeks of harvest. Let some flower for coriander seed. Save for fall. - Carrot — Direct sow OK now, but they prefer cooler soil. Deep container with loose mix, barely below surface, 10–14 days to germinate. Save for Fall (August–September Start) - Broccoli — Cool-season. Spring start = May transplant = bolts before heading. Start indoors August, transplant September. - Onion (Sweet Spanish) — Onion seed needs October–January start in Houston. Buy onion sets (small bulbs) for spring. Already Planted / Perennials - Spearmint and Lavender — Established outdoors. Apply Myco Supreme to root zone now. Mycorrhizal fungi dramatically improve nutrient/water uptake (especially for lavender). My Recommended Allocation - Outdoor containers: Okra, both basils, cucumber. - Indoor nursery: Tomato, pepper, jalapeño, rosemary, lettuce, cilantro. - Hydroponics (future): Lettuce (Gourmet Blend). - Potato tower: Need actual seed potatoes (not from packet) — get from nursery. - Hold for fall: Broccoli, onion seed, carrot, second lettuce/cilantro round. - Space-dependent: Corn (4×4 minimum), watermelon (6+ ft sprawl), cantaloupe — patio-only is a tough grow. --- Links: Garden Monitor · Outdoor Watering System · Indoor Nursery · Outdoor Garden Layout #garden-monitor #planting #houston #zone-9a #seasonal

title: Wiring Guide
body: Step-by-step beginner wiring guide for the Garden Monitor project. ⚠️ Always wire with the Arduino unplugged from USB/power . --- What You Need for This Step | Item | Qty | Notes | |------|-----|-------| | Arduino Mega 2560 | 1 | The big blue board | | Gikfun Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor v1.2 | 2 | The black PCB sticks | | Jumper wires (female-to-male) | 6 | 3 wires per sensor | | USB Type-B cable | 1 | To connect Mega to your PC (and later to Pi 5) | | A cup of water + dry soil | — | For calibration testing | --- Understanding the Sensor Your Gikfun capacitive soil moisture sensor v1.2 has 3 wires coming from a connector: | Wire Color | Label on PCB | What It Does | |-----------|-------------|-------------| | Red | VCC | Power (3.3V or 5V) | | Black | GND | Ground | | Yellow | AOUT | Analog signal output (the moisture reading) | The sensor outputs a voltage on the yellow wire that changes based on moisture: - Dry air/soil → higher number (around 500–600) - Wet soil/water → lower number (around 200–300) 💡 Capacitive sensors are better than the cheap metal-prong ones because they don't corrode over time in wet soil. --- Understanding the Arduino Mega Pins Looking at the Arduino Mega with the USB port facing LEFT: We need: - A0 — Analog pin for Sensor 1 (Lavender zone) - A1 — Analog pin for Sensor 2 (Potato tower zone) - 5V — Power for both sensors - GND — Ground for both sensors --- Step-by-Step Wiring Sensor 1 — Lavender Zone (Zone 2) | Sensor Wire | → | Arduino Mega Pin | How to Find It | |------------|---|-----------------|----------------| | Red (VCC) | → | 5V | Bottom-left power cluster, labeled "5V" | | Black (GND) | → | GND | Right next to 5V, labeled "GND" | | Yellow (AOUT) | → | A0 | Bottom edge, first analog pin, labeled "A0" | Sensor 2 — Potato Tower (Zone 4) | Sensor Wire | → | Arduino Mega Pin | How to Find It | |------------|---|-----------------|----------------| | Red (VCC) | → | 5V | Same 5V pin (can share with Sensor 1) | | Black (GND) | → | GND | Same GND pin (can share with Sensor 1) | | Yellow (AOUT) | → | A1 | Bottom edge, second analog pin, labeled "A1" | 💡 Sharing power pins is fine. Both sensors draw very little current. You can plug both red wires into the same 5V pin and both black wires into the same GND pin. If it's physically difficult, the Mega has multiple GND pins — use any of them. --- Wiring Diagram (Visual) ![Soil moisture sensor wiring to Arduino Mega 2560](/ assets/wiring-soil-sensors.svg) Wiring Diagram (Text Version) --- After Wiring — Quick Checklist - [ ] Red wires go to 5V (NOT 3.3V — these sensors work better at 5V with the Mega) - [ ] Black wires go to GND - [ ] Yellow wire from Sensor 1 goes to A0 - [ ] Yellow wire from Sensor 2 goes to A1 - [ ] No wires are touching each other where they shouldn't - [ ] USB cable is plugged into the Mega's USB-B port - [ ] The other end of the USB cable goes to your PC (for now) or Pi 5 (later) --- Next Step → Go to Arduino Setup Guide to install the Arduino IDE and upload the sensor reading code. --- Links: Garden Monitor · Outdoor Watering System · Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor · Arduino Mega · Arduino Setup Guide #garden-monitor #wiring #beginner

title: Arduino Setup Guide
body: Step-by-step guide to install the Arduino IDE, upload code, and read soil moisture sensors. Part of the Garden Monitor project. --- Overview — What We're Building By the end of this guide, your Arduino Mega will: 1. Read 2 soil moisture sensors every 5 seconds 2. Print the readings to the Serial Monitor (so you can see them on your PC) 3. Send JSON-formatted data over USB serial (so the Pi 5 can read them later) 4. Blink the onboard LED when it takes a reading (so you know it's working) --- Part 1: Install Arduino IDE Step 1 — Download 1. Go to https://www.arduino.cc/en/software 2. Download Arduino IDE 2.x for Windows 3. Run the installer, accept defaults, click through Step 2 — First Launch 1. Open Arduino IDE 2. It will download some initial packages — let it finish 3. You should see a blank sketch with setup() and loop() Step 3 — Connect Your Arduino Mega 1. Plug the USB-B cable into the Mega and into your PC 2. In Arduino IDE, look at the top toolbar — you should see a dropdown that says something like: - Arduino Mega or Mega 2560 on COM3 (the COM number may vary) 3. If it says "No board selected": - Click the dropdown → Select board → Search for "Mega" - Select Arduino Mega or Mega 2560 - Select the COM port that appeared when you plugged in 💡 Not seeing a COM port? You may need the CH340 USB driver if your Mega is a clone. Search "CH340 driver download" and install it. --- Part 2: Upload the Sensor Reading Code Step 4 — Create a New Sketch 1. In Arduino IDE: File → New Sketch 2. Delete everything in the editor 3. Copy and paste the entire code below (also saved at Software/Arduino/garden monitor sensors.ino in this vault) Here is the complete code: Step 5 — Upload the Code 1. Make sure your Mega is selected in the board dropdown (top toolbar) 2. Click the → (Upload) button (right arrow icon in the top-left) 3. You'll see: - "Compiling sketch..." (wait 10–20 seconds) - "Uploading..." (a few seconds) - "Done uploading." ← success! ⚠️ If you get an error, check: Is the correct board selected? Is the correct COM port selected? Is the USB cable a data cable (not charge-only)? Step 6 — Open the Serial Monitor 1. Click Tools → Serial Monitor (or the magnifying glass icon top-right) 2. Make sure the baud rate dropdown at the bottom says 9600 3. You should see output like: 🎉 If you see JSON lines appearing every 5 seconds, your wiring is correct and the code is working! --- Part 3: Calibrate Your Sensors The raw readings will only mean something useful after you calibrate them with YOUR soil. Step 7 — Dry Air Baseline 1. Hold both sensors in the open air (not touching anything) 2. Note the raw values — they should be around 550–600 3. Write down the number: DRY AIR VALUE = Step 8 — Water Baseline 1. Put both sensors in a cup of water (only the black PCB part — keep the connector and wires DRY) 2. Note the raw values — they should drop to around 200–280 3. Write down the number: WATER VALUE = Step 9 — Update Calibration in Code 1. In the Arduino code, find these lines near the top: 2. Replace the numbers with YOUR measured values 3. Re-upload the code (click Upload again) Step 10 — Soil Test 1. Stick Sensor 1 into the lavender pot soil 2. Stick Sensor 2 into the potato tower soil 3. Watch the readings — the percentage should now show a meaningful 0–100% moisture level 4. Water the soil a bit and watch the numbers change — they should go UP toward 100% 5. title: Outdoor Watering System
body: Detailed system design for automated watering of 4 plant zones on the south side of the house in Houston, TX. Part of the Garden Monitor project · See also System Architecture --- Site Overview - Location: South side of house, Houston TX (USDA Zone 9a) - Sun exposure: ~6–7 hours direct sun per day - Climate: Hot, humid subtropical — summers routinely 95–100°F with high humidity - Key challenge: Houston heat + humidity means plants can cook if overwatered (wet foliage + heat = fungal death), but potted plants dry out fast in direct sun --- The 4 Zones Zone 1 — Spearmint (1 plant, single pot) Watering profile: HIGH moisture demand - Mint needs consistently moist soil — it wilts visibly when thirsty but rebounds fast - In Houston summer heat, potted mint may need watering daily or every other day - In scorching Texas summers, mint often goes into "hibernation" and looks rough — it'll come back when temps cool - Water at the base, keep foliage dry to prevent fungal issues (rust is common on mint in Houston) - Let the top inch dry between waterings, but don't let it go bone dry Sensor strategy: 1 × Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor Threshold: Water when reading drops below "moist soil" calibration (~350–400 range, TBD after calibration) Watering duration: Short burst — 10–15 seconds of pump flow, then wait and re-check Special notes: - Mulch the pot to reduce evaporation - Consider afternoon shade if plant struggles in peak summer - Spearmint in a pot in Houston = daily water monitoring is critical --- Zone 2 — Lavender (3 plants, rectangle pot) Watering profile: LOW moisture demand — the opposite of mint - Lavender is Mediterranean — it wants to be dry between waterings - In Houston's humidity, lavender is more likely to die from overwatering than underwatering - Water deeply but infrequently — once a week at most when established, maybe less - The saying from Texas lavender growers: "If you think it needs water, wait until tomorrow" - Water at the base ONLY — wet foliage + Houston humidity = black leaves and death - Mulch with gravel or expanded shale (NOT organic mulch) to keep lower foliage dry and reflect heat - Excellent drainage is absolutely critical — the rectangle pot needs drainage holes and fast-draining soil mix (sand/perlite heavy) Sensor strategy: 1 × Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor (shared across the rectangle pot) Threshold: Water ONLY when reading drops well into "dry soil" range (~450–500+, TBD) Watering duration: Deep soak — 20–30 seconds of pump flow, then don't water again for days Cooldown period: Minimum 4–5 days between waterings , enforced in firmware Special notes: - Best lavender varieties for Houston: Sweet Lavender, Fern Leaf, or French/Spanish types - Don't expect lavender to last more than 2–3 years in Houston — it's not their climate - Don't over-fertilize — lavender likes lean soil - ⚠️ This zone needs the OPPOSITE logic from mint — the system must prevent accidental overwatering --- Zone 3 — Citronella (1 plant, single pot) Watering profile: MODERATE moisture demand - Citronella (scented geranium / Pelargonium citrosum) is drought-tolerant but appreciates regular moisture - Water when the top inch of soil is dry — roughly every 2–3 days in Houston summer - Good drainage is essential — citronella gets root rot from standing water - Can handle Houston's heat and humidity reasonably well - Benefits from afternoon shade in peak summer - Fertilize container-grown citronella biweekly during growing season Sensor strategy: Share sensor data with Zone 1 OR dedicate a sensor if budget allows (we only have 2 sensors currently — see [Sensor Allocation](#sensor-allocation) below) Threshold: Water when reading drops to "moderately dry" range (~400–440, TBD) Watering duration: Medium — 12–18 seconds of pump flow Special notes: - Citronella is toxic to pets — placement matters if dogs/cats are around - Pinch tips regularly for bushier, more fragrant growth - Bring indoors before first frost (typically late Novembe

title: System Architecture
body: How all the hardware and software connects in Garden Monitor. --- Architecture Documents - Outdoor Watering System — Detailed 4-zone irrigation design with per-plant watering profiles, sensor allocation, firmware logic, physical layout, and Houston-specific considerations - This page — Overall system connectivity and communication --- High-Level Overview --- Communication Protocols | From | To | Protocol | Data | |------|----|----------|------| | Soil Moisture Sensors | Arduino Mega | Analog wire | Voltage (moisture) | | Arduino Nicla Sense Env | Arduino Mega | I2C | Temp, humidity, gas | | Arduino Mega | Raspberry Pi 5 | USB Serial (UART) | JSON sensor packets | | Arduino Nicla Vision | Raspberry Pi 5 | WiFi (HTTP/MQTT) | Images, health alerts | | Raspberry Pi 5 | Arduino Mega | USB Serial | Watering commands per zone | | Raspberry Pi 5 | ESP Display 5in | WiFi (MQTT) | Dashboard data | | Raspberry Pi 5 | Phone/PC | WiFi (HTTP) | Web dashboard | --- Data Flow 1. Sense — Soil moisture per zone (analog), temp/humidity/gas (I2C), soil temp (future DS18B20) 2. Collect — Arduino Mega polls sensors every 5 min, packages as JSON, sends over serial 3. Process — Pi 5 receives data, stores in DB, evaluates per-zone thresholds 4. Act — Per-zone watering decisions: open correct solenoid valve + run pump for zone-specific duration 5. Display — Dashboard updates on ESP Display 5in and/or web UI with per-zone status 6. Alert — Push notification if: pump failure, sensor offline, potato soil temp too high, reservoir low --- Resolved Questions - [x] ~~MQTT vs REST for ESP Display~~ → MQTT (lightweight, real-time push updates) - [x] ~~Where do Pi 1B boards fit~~ → Shelved for now, Pi 5 handles everything - [x] ~~Keep GIGA Display Shield~~ → Shelved, ESP Display 5in is primary display (self-contained WiFi) - [ ] Power plan for outdoor components → See Outdoor Watering System#Power Plan - [ ] Weatherproofing strategy → IP65 junction box, cable glands, covered reservoir --- Links: Garden Monitor · Outdoor Watering System · Hardware Inventory #garden-monitor #architecture #planning
